case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old woman was evaluated for generalized dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, severe scoliosis, and motor development disorder that began in her childhood. Born by cesarean delivery to nonconsanguineous parents, she developed difficulties with head control, standing, and feeding at age 10 months. Subsequently, she faced progressive motor challenges (walking, speech, and swallow); contractures in her fingers, toes, wrists, and knees; and scoliosis. In adolescence, she experienced progressive stiffness, episodes of painful spasms and oculomotor crisis, and galactorrhea unrelated to childbirth in adulthood. Her symptoms worsened with age and progressed to her using a wheelchair, having difficulty in speech, and not having access to education. She had a younger brother with similar symptoms who passed away at age 20 years of unknown causes. Upon presentation at age 31 years, she was admitted to our center for further evaluation. She had thin limbs and was of standard height. The neurological and psychological examinations revealed scoliosis, contractures in her fingers and toes, carpal inversion, dysarthria, dysphagia, hypertonia, decreased tendon reflexes, absence of Babinski sign (Figure, A and B), and no psychiatric problems. Blood test results indicated hyperprolactinemia (prolactin level of 47.40 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1). An electroencephalogram revealed atypical spike-slow wave synchronization in specific brain regions during sleep. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant global atrophy particularly in her anterior temporal, lateral, and frontal regions (Figure, C). Levodopa treatment was initiated but quickly resulted in drug-induced hyperkinesia (Video).

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD.    - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,

  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,

}

Her symptoms worsened with age and progressed to her using a wheelchair, having difficulty in speech, and not having access to education. She had a younger brother with similar symptoms who passed away at age 20 years of unknown causes. Upon presentation at age 31 years, she was admitted to our center for further evaluation. case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old woman was evaluated for generalized dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, severe scoliosis, and motor development disorder that began in her childhood. Born by cesarean delivery to nonconsanguineous parents, she developed difficulties with head control, standing, and feeding at age 10 months. Subsequently, she faced progressive motor challenges (walking, speech, and swallow); contractures in her fingers, toes, wrists, and knees; and scoliosis. In adolescence, she experienced progressive stiffness, episodes of painful spasms and oculomotor crisis, and galactorrhea unrelated to childbirth in adulthood. Her symptoms worsened with age and progressed to her using a wheelchair, having difficulty in speech, and not having access to education. She had a younger brother with similar symptoms who passed away at age 20 years of unknown causes. Upon presentation at age 31 years, she was admitted to our center for further evaluation. She had thin limbs and was of standard height. The neurological and psychological examinations revealed scoliosis, contractures in her fingers and toes, carpal inversion, dysarthria, dysphagia, hypertonia, decreased tendon reflexes, absence of Babinski sign (Figure, A and B), and no psychiatric problems. Blood test results indicated hyperprolactinemia (prolactin level of 47.40 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1). An electroencephalogram revealed atypical spike-slow wave synchronization in specific brain regions during sleep. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant global atrophy particularly in her anterior temporal, lateral, and frontal regions (Figure, C). Levodopa treatment was initiated but quickly resulted in drug-induced hyperkinesia (Video).
case_info.caption: A, Characteristic features of hypertonia. A 31-year-old woman with flexion contracture of the fingers and carpal inversion. B, Severe scoliosis. C, Brain magnetic resonance imaging showing prominent atrophy in the anterior, lateral temporal, and frontal regions.
case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old woman was evaluated for generalized dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, severe scoliosis, and motor development disorder that began in her childhood. Born by cesarean delivery to nonconsanguineous parents, she developed difficulties with head control, standing, and feeding at age 10 months. Subsequently, she faced progressive motor challenges (walking, speech, and swallow); contractures in her fingers, toes, wrists, and knees; and scoliosis. In adolescence, she experienced progressive stiffness, episodes of painful spasms and oculomotor crisis, and galactorrhea unrelated to childbirth in adulthood. Her symptoms worsened with age and progressed to her using a wheelchair, having difficulty in speech, and not having access to education. She had a younger brother with similar symptoms who passed away at age 20 years of unknown causes. Upon presentation at age 31 years, she was admitted to our center for further evaluation. She had thin limbs and was of standard height. The neurological and psychological examinations revealed scoliosis, contractures in her fingers and toes, carpal inversion, dysarthria, dysphagia, hypertonia, decreased tendon reflexes, absence of Babinski sign (Figure, A and B), and no psychiatric problems. Blood test results indicated hyperprolactinemia (prolactin level of 47.40 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1). An electroencephalogram revealed atypical spike-slow wave synchronization in specific brain regions during sleep. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant global atrophy particularly in her anterior temporal, lateral, and frontal regions (Figure, C). Levodopa treatment was initiated but quickly resulted in drug-induced hyperkinesia (Video).
case_info.caption: A, Characteristic features of hypertonia. A 31-year-old woman with flexion contracture of the fingers and carpal inversion. B, Severe scoliosis. C, Brain magnetic resonance imaging showing prominent atrophy in the anterior, lateral temporal, and frontal regions.
case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

[Case]
A 31-year-old woman was evaluated for generalized dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, severe scoliosis, and motor development disorder that began in her childhood. Born by cesarean delivery to nonconsanguineous parents, she developed difficulties with head control, standing, and feeding at age 10 months. Subsequently, she faced progressive motor challenges (walking, speech, and swallow); contractures in her fingers, toes, wrists, and knees; and scoliosis. In adolescence, she experienced progressive stiffness, episodes of painful spasms and oculomotor crisis, and galactorrhea unrelated to childbirth in adulthood. Her symptoms worsened with age and progressed to her using a wheelchair, having difficulty in speech, and not having access to education. She had a younger brother with similar symptoms who passed away at age 20 years of unknown causes. Upon presentation at age 31 years, she was admitted to our center for further evaluation. She had thin limbs and was of standard height. The neurological and psychological examinations revealed scoliosis, contractures in her fingers and toes, carpal inversion, dysarthria, dysphagia, hypertonia, decreased tendon reflexes, absence of Babinski sign (Figure, A and B), and no psychiatric problems. Blood test results indicated hyperprolactinemia (prolactin level of 47.40 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1). An electroencephalogram revealed atypical spike-slow wave synchronization in specific brain regions during sleep. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant global atrophy particularly in her anterior temporal, lateral, and frontal regions (Figure, C). Levodopa treatment was initiated but quickly resulted in drug-induced hyperkinesia (Video).
